title: Narcissism: But what about me?
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant explore narcissism: the Narcissus myth and the origin of the word, its early history in sexology and psychoanalysis (Havelock Ellis, Otto Rank, Freud, Wilhelm Reich, Karen Horney, Annie Reich, Henry Murray's covert narcissism, Paul Wink's typology), its entry into the DSM as narcissistic personality disorder, the debate over Big Five trait models versus categorical personality disorders, the DSM criteria, causes (nature vs. nurture, parenting and the self-esteem craze), Jean Twenge's "Narcissism Epidemic" claims about rising narcissism and baby names, data disputes (college NPI samples, Monitoring the Future), prevalence uncertainty, treatment difficulties, narcissism in the workplace, brain and empathy studies, and whether social media signals rising narcissism. The episode closes with a listener mail about Shope papillomavirus in rabbits and the Shope/HPV connection.

segments.title: Opening banter and Facebook live announcement
segments.summary: Josh announces an upcoming Facebook live about Movie Crush, and the hosts banter about two-dollar bills, subliminal messages, and the idea of short episodes.

segments.title: Personal take on narcissism and definitions
segments.summary: The hosts discuss whether they relate to narcissism traits, define narcissism experientially and clinically, and note that psychology defines normal by how well people fit into society and that the term has been diluted by pop culture.

segments.title: Myth of Narcissus
segments.summary: Retelling of the Narcissus myth: the prophet Teiresias warns his parents, Narcissus rejects admirers including Echo, Nemesis punishes him, and he falls in love with his reflection and becomes a flower. The hosts note the myth's use as an allegory for a personality type.

segments.title: Clinical definition and two sides of narcissism
segments.summary: The classic clinical picture of a narcissist is described: inflated self-importance, entitlement, trouble with criticism, and fragile underlying self-esteem, with the hosts noting there are two sides to the narcissism coin.

segments.title: Early history: Ellis, Rank, and Freud
segments.summary: Havelock Ellis linked narcissism to masturbation in the late 1890s, Otto Rank in 1911 broadened it to general self-obsession, and Freud in 1914 framed it as a phase everyone passes through, which becomes a true disorder only if not outgrown.

segments.title: Reich, Horney, and Annie Reich
segments.summary: Robert Waelder treated narcissism as a personality type, Wilhelm Reich linked it to masculinity and aggression, Karen Horney in 1939 called narcissism a defense against insecurity, and Annie Reich in 1960 tied it to childhood vulnerability and an all-or-nothing outlook.

segments.title: Covert and overt narcissism typologies
segments.summary: Henry Murray described covert narcissists who are introverted and anxious, Paul Wink later classified types into grandiosity, exhibitionism, and vulnerability sensitivity, with delusions of persecution as a key feature. Both types center on the self.

segments.title: Entry into the DSM
segments.summary: Otto Kernberg coined narcissistic character disorder in 1961 and Heinz Kohut described narcissistic personality disorder in 1968 (as stated in the episode), which entered the DSM-III in 1980. The hosts note the DSM-5 debate between categorical disorders and the Big Five trait model.

segments.title: Ad break
segments.summary: Sponsor break in the middle of the episode.

segments.title: DSM criteria, causes, and the self-esteem craze
segments.summary: The nine DSM criteria for narcissistic personality disorder are listed, with the hosts noting five of nine are needed. Causes are discussed as nature and nurture, including parenting, and a book on the self-esteem movement is mentioned.

segments.title: Narcissism epidemic debate and data
segments.summary: Jean Twenge and W. Keith Campbell's The Narcissism Epidemic is discussed, including baby-name trivia used as evidence. The hosts discuss the debate over whether narcissism is rising, citing a large self-report study, college NPI samples, and Monitoring the Future data showing little change, and argue that social media may reflect social change rather than a rise.

segments.title: Listener mail on Shope papilloma virus in rabbits
segments.summary: Listener Jane Niemeyer writes that Richard Shope isolated the virus causing horn-like growths in rabbits in the Twin Cities, a virus related to human papillomavirus and the HPV vaccine.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank the listener and give social media and website contact information.
